When a study is noisy, only the estimates that happen to come out large clear the $p < 0.05$ bar ($|\hat\theta| > 1.96\,\text{se}$). This lab builds Gelman and Carlin's (2014) **design analysis** from scratch in base R so you can measure how much the significance filter exaggerates true effects (**Type M error**) and how often it flips their sign (**Type S error**).

## Step 1: One study, replicated 400 times

Suppose a treatment has a true effect of `theta <- 0.2`, and each study estimates it with standard error `se <- 0.25`. At this noise level, the study has only 13% power. Run the code below, then try the three experiments underneath it.

```{webr}
set.seed(42)
theta <- 0.2 # true effect
se <- 0.25 # standard error of each study
n_rep <- 400 # number of replications

est <- rnorm(n_rep, mean = theta, sd = se)
sig <- abs(est) > 1.96 * se # statistically significant at the 5% level

power <- 1 - pnorm(1.96 - theta / se) + pnorm(-1.96 - theta / se)
avg_sig <- mean(abs(est[sig]))
wrong_sign <- sum(sign(est[sig]) != sign(theta))

cat(
  "Power: ", round(100 * power, 1), "%\n",
  "Significant replications: ", sum(sig), " of ", n_rep, "\n",
  "Average |estimate| when significant: ", round(avg_sig, 2),
  " (truth = ", theta, ")\n",
  "Exaggeration ratio (Type M): ", round(avg_sig / theta, 1), "x\n",
  "Significant with the wrong sign (Type S): ", wrong_sign, "\n",
  sep = ""
)

plot(est,
  pch = ifelse(sig, 19, 1), col = ifelse(sig, "#d6604d", "grey65"),
  xlab = "Replication", ylab = "Estimated effect"
)
abline(h = c(-1.96, 1.96) * se, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
abline(h = theta, col = "#2166ac", lwd = 2)
abline(h = 0)
```

::: {.lab-experiments}
<strong class="lab-exp-title"><i class="bi bi-sliders" aria-hidden="true"></i> Predict → Modify → Observe</strong>

1. **Shrink the true effect.** Before editing, predict: if you cut `theta` from `0.2` to `0.05` (keeping `se <- 0.25`), will the average significant estimate `avg_sig` drop toward `0.05`? Change `theta <- 0.05` on line 2 and click **Run Code**. Notice that `avg_sig` stays stuck above `0.50`—because the significance threshold `1.96 * se = 0.49` sets a hard floor on what can be called "significant", inflating the exaggeration ratio past $10\times$.
2. **Count the wrong-sign "discoveries".** At `theta <- 0.05`, check the last printed line: how many statistically significant estimates point in the *opposite* direction of the true effect?
3. **Shrink the noise instead.** Keep `theta <- 0.2` and lower `se` from `0.25` to `0.07` (which requires $(0.25 / 0.07)^2 \approx 13$ times as many participants). Watch how the gray dead-zone narrows and the exaggeration ratio drops near `1.1x`.
:::

## Step 2: How exaggeration grows as power falls

One batch of 400 replications has Monte Carlo noise. Gelman and Carlin's [design analysis](https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691614551642) computes the expected exaggeration ratio across a whole grid of plausible true effects `thetas` for a fixed standard error `se = 0.25`.

```{webr}
exaggeration <- function(theta, se, n_sims = 5e4) {
  est <- rnorm(n_sims, mean = theta, sd = se)
  sig <- abs(est) > 1.96 * se
  mean(abs(est[sig])) / theta
}

se <- 0.25
thetas <- seq(0.05, 1.0, by = 0.05)
power <- 1 - pnorm(1.96 - thetas / se) + pnorm(-1.96 - thetas / se)
set.seed(32)
ratio <- sapply(thetas, exaggeration, se = se)

plot(100 * power, ratio,
  type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#2166ac", log = "y",
  xlab = "Statistical power (%)", ylab = "Exaggeration ratio (log scale)"
)
abline(h = c(1, 1.5, 2, 5), lty = 2, col = "grey60")
round(
  data.frame(theta = thetas, power_pct = 100 * power, type_m = ratio)[
    c(1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 20),
  ],
  2
)
```

## Your turn: compute the exact Type S (wrong-sign) rate

When $\theta > 0$ and $\hat\theta \sim \mathrm{N}(\theta, \text{se}^2)$, you don't even need random numbers to find the **Type S error rate**—the probability that a statistically significant estimate is negative ($\hat\theta < -1.96\,\text{se}$).

Complete the function `type_s(theta, se)` below using `pPos` (the chance of a significant positive estimate) and `pNeg` (the chance of a significant negative estimate), then compute the Type S rate when `theta = 0.1` and `se = 0.25`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_type_s
#| setup: true
# Clean environment for the exercise
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_type_s
#| autorun: false
type_s <- function(theta, se) {
  p_pos <- 1 - pnorm(1.96 - theta / se) # Pr(est > +1.96 * se)
  p_neg <- pnorm(-1.96 - theta / se) # Pr(est < -1.96 * se)
  # Return the share of significant estimates that are negative:
  ______
}

# Test at theta = 0.1, se = 0.25 (power is about 7%):
round(100 * type_s(theta = 0.1, se = 0.25), 1)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_type_s"}
An estimate is significant with Probability `p_pos + p_neg`, and it has the wrong sign (negative when `theta > 0`) with probability `p_neg`. Divide `p_neg` by the total probability of significance `p_pos + p_neg`.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_type_s
#| solution: true
type_s <- function(theta, se) {
  p_pos <- 1 - pnorm(1.96 - theta / se) # Pr(est > +1.96 * se)
  p_neg <- pnorm(-1.96 - theta / se) # Pr(est < -1.96 * se)
  p_neg / (p_pos + p_neg)
}

# At theta = 0.1, se = 0.25, ~9% of significant findings have the wrong sign:
round(100 * type_s(theta = 0.1, se = 0.25), 1)
```
